MARITAL SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE
This Marital Settlement Agreement is entered into by Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, who were married on June 14, 2015 and who separated on March 2, 2026, for the purpose of resolving the division of their property and debts, and, where applicable, support and parenting matters, arising from the dissolution of their marriage.

EQUAL DIVISION OF COMMUNITY ESTATE (DEFAULT RULE)
Except upon the written agreement of Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, or their oral stipulation in open court, or as otherwise provided by statute, a court presiding over a dissolution of marriage or legal separation is required to divide the community estate of the parties equally. This agreement, if it allocates community property other than by an equal in-kind division, is an exercise of that written-agreement exception.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except upon the written agreement of the parties, or on oral stipulation of the parties in open court, or as otherwise provided in this division, in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties, the court shall, either in its judgment of dissolution of the marriage, in its judgment of legal separation of the parties, or at a later time if it expressly reserves jurisdiction to make such a property division, divide the community estate of the parties equally."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2550 (California Legislative Information text), the equal-division default rule and its written-agreement exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2550.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how community-property jurisdictions default to equal division of marital estates — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marital settlement agreement. Community property is itself a minority framework among U.S. states; many states divide marital property under an "equitable distribution" standard instead, which does not start from a 50/50 baseline. This is a single statutory section (§ 2550); no additional independent source was found for this.

COMMUNITY PROPERTY VS. SEPARATE PROPERTY
Property acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in this state is generally community property, except as otherwise provided by statute. Separate property includes all property owned by a spouse before marriage, all property acquired after marriage by gift, bequest, devise, or descent, and the rents, issues, and profits of such property. This agreement's characterization of specific assets and debts as community or separate property of Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee draws on this statutory framework.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except as otherwise provided by statute, all property, real or personal, wherever situated, acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in this state is community property."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 760 (California Legislative Information text), the community property default (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=760.)
  "Separate property of a married person includes all of the following: (1) All property owned by the person before marriage. (2) All property acquired by the person after marriage by gift, bequest, devise, or descent. (3) The rents, issues, and profits of the property described in this section."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 770(a) (California Legislative Information text), the separate property definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=770.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one community-property jurisdiction distinguishes community from separate property — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marital settlement agreement. Characterization rules, presumptions, and their exceptions (commingling, transmutation, tracing) vary significantly by state and are fact-specific; this clause states the general statutory categories only.

DATE OF SEPARATION AND POST-SEPARATION EARNINGS
"Date of separation" means the date a complete and final break in the marital relationship has occurred, as evidenced by both (1) a spouse expressing to the other spouse the intent to end the marriage, and (2) conduct of that spouse consistent with that intent; a court considers all relevant evidence in making this determination. The parties identify March 2, 2026 as the date of separation for purposes of this agreement. The earnings and accumulations of a spouse (and of minor children living with or in that spouse's custody) after the date of separation are that spouse's separate property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "“Date of separation” means the date that a complete and final break in the marital relationship has occurred, as evidenced by both of the following: (1) The spouse has expressed to the other spouse the intent to end the marriage. (2) The conduct of the spouse is consistent with the intent to end the marriage. (b) In determining the date of separation, the court shall take into consideration all relevant evidence. (c) It is the intent of the Legislature in enacting this section to abrogate the decisions in In re Marriage of Davis (2015) 61 Cal.4th 846 and In re Marriage of Norviel (2002) 102 Cal.App.4th 1152."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 70(a)-(c) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory test for date of separation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=70.)
  "The earnings and accumulations of a spouse and the minor children living with, or in the custody of, the spouse, after the date of separation of the spouses, are the separate property of the spouse."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 771(a) (California Legislative Information text), post-separation earnings are separate property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=771.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction defines "date of separation" and its consequence for post-separation earnings — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marital settlement agreement. This is a specific, litigated statutory test (the Legislature enacted it in 2015 to abrogate the California Supreme Court's contrary holding in In re Marriage of Davis), and comparable concepts in other states carry different names, tests, and effective dates entirely.

PROPERTY DIVISION SCHEDULE
The parties' community and separate property and debts, and the manner of their division between Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, are set forth in the attached property schedule(s) incorporated into this agreement by reference. ☐ Property schedule attached.

FACTORS A COURT CONSIDERS IN ORDERING SPOUSAL SUPPORT
In ordering spousal support, a court is directed to consider all of the following circumstances: the marketable skills of the supported party and the job market for those skills; the extent to which the supported party's earning capacity was impaired by periods of unemployment incurred during the marriage to permit devotion of time to domestic duties; the extent to which the supported party contributed to the supporting party's education, training, career position, or license; the supporting party's ability to pay, considering earning capacity, income, assets, and standard of living; the needs of each party based on the marital standard of living; the obligations and assets, including separate property, of each party; the duration of the marriage; the supported party's ability to work without unduly interfering with the interests of dependent children in that party's custody; the age and health of the parties; documented evidence of domestic violence between the parties; tax consequences to each party; the balance of hardships to each party; the goal that the supported party become self-supporting within a reasonable period of time (generally one-half the length of the marriage, except for a marriage of long duration); and any other factors the court determines are just and equitable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "In ordering spousal support under this part, the court shall consider all of the following circumstances: (a) The extent to which the earning capacity of each party is sufficient to maintain the standard of living established during the marriage... (l) The goal that the supported party shall be self-supporting within a reasonable period of time. Except in the case of a marriage of long duration as described in Section 4336, a "reasonable period of time" for purposes of this section generally shall be one-half the length of the marriage."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4320(a)-(l) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory factor list for spousal support (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4320.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the kind of factor list a court applies to spousal support — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marital settlement agreement, and not advice about how these factors apply to any specific marriage. Both the existence of a factor-based standard and the "one-half the length of the marriage" self-support benchmark are jurisdiction-specific; many states use different frameworks (formulaic guidelines, different factor lists, or no comparable benchmark at all) for spousal or "alimony" support. This is a single statutory section (§ 4320); no additional independent source was found for this.

THE "LONG DURATION" MARRIAGE PRESUMPTION (10-YEAR RULE)
Except on written agreement of the parties to the contrary or a court order terminating spousal support, a court retains jurisdiction indefinitely over spousal support in a dissolution or legal separation proceeding where the marriage is of long duration. For this purpose, a rebuttable presumption applies that a marriage of 10 years or more, measured from the date of marriage to the date of separation, is a marriage of long duration; a court may also determine that a marriage of less than 10 years is of long duration, and may consider periods of separation during the marriage in making that determination. The parties identify June 14, 2015 as the date of marriage and March 2, 2026 as the date of separation for purposes of this agreement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) Except on written agreement of the parties to the contrary or a court order terminating spousal support, the court retains jurisdiction indefinitely in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties where the marriage is of long duration. (b) For the purpose of retaining jurisdiction, there is a presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence that a marriage of 10 years or more, from the date of marriage to the date of separation, is a marriage of long duration. However, the court may consider periods of separation during the marriage in determining whether the marriage is in fact of long duration. Nothing in this subdivision precludes a court from determining that a marriage of less than 10 years is a marriage of long duration."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4336(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the long-duration-marriage presumption and indefinite jurisdiction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4336.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific "10-year marriage" jurisdiction-retention rule for spousal support — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marital settlement agreement. The presumption is expressly rebuttable, not automatic, and the 10-year threshold, the indefinite-jurisdiction consequence, and the ability to contract around it by written agreement are all particular to this jurisdiction's statute. This is a single statutory section (§ 4336); no additional independent source was found for this.

CUSTODY AND VISITATION STIPULATIONS REMAIN SUBJECT TO BEST-INTEREST REVIEW
A statutory presumption favors joint custody as being in a child's best interest where the parents have agreed to joint custody, or so agree in open court at a custody hearing — but that presumption operates subject to the court's best-interest analysis. Where parents stipulate in writing or on the record regarding custody or visitation, the statute does not eliminate the requirement that the contents of the stipulation be in the best interest of the child and be specific as to the time, day, place, and manner of transfer of the child. Any custody or visitation terms in this agreement concerning children of Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee are subject to that same court review and are not self-executing by agreement alone.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "There is a presumption, affecting the burden of proof, that joint custody is in the best interest of a minor child, subject to Section 3011, where the parents have agreed to joint custody or so agree in open court at a hearing for the purpose of determining the custody of the minor child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3080 (California Legislative Information text), the joint-custody agreement presumption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3080.)
  "Nothing in this paragraph eliminates the requirement that the contents of the stipulation be in the best interest of the child and be specific as to time, day, place, and manner of transfer of the child if the parties do stipulate in writing or on the record regarding custody or visitation."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3011(a)(5)(B) (California Legislative Information text), a custody stipulation still must be in the child's best interest (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3011.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that parental custody agreements remain subject to a court's independent best-interest review rather than being enforceable purely by private contract — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marital settlement agreement. Best-interest standards, the weight given to parental agreement, and joint-custody presumptions all vary by state; this document does not address the fuller custody-factor scheme, which is covered separately.

PRIVATE AGREEMENT VS. ENFORCEABLE COURT JUDGMENT
A written settlement between parties to pending litigation may, upon motion, be entered by the court as a judgment on the terms of that settlement, where the parties have stipulated to the settlement in a signed writing or orally before the court. Family law property-division judgments are themselves entered as part of "its judgment of dissolution of the marriage" or "its judgment of legal separation," rather than arising automatically from a private agreement standing alone. This agreement between Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee states the parties' negotiated terms; whether and how it is presented to a court for entry as a judgment is a separate procedural step from the agreement's execution.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "the court shall, either in its judgment of dissolution of the marriage, in its judgment of legal separation of the parties, or at a later time if it expressly reserves jurisdiction to make such a property division, divide the community estate of the parties equally"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2550 (California Legislative Information text), property-division judgments are entered as part of the dissolution/separation judgment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2550.)
  "If parties to pending litigation stipulate, in a writing signed by the parties outside of the presence of the court or orally before the court, for settlement of the case, or part thereof, the court, upon motion, may enter judgment pursuant to the terms of the settlement."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 664.6(a) (California Legislative Information text), the general mechanism for entering a stipulated settlement as a judgment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=664.6.)
  Known gap: This is a mix of a Family Code provision and a general Code of Civil Procedure statute governing settlements, not one clean, dedicated statutory section stating that marital settlement agreements specifically must be "incorporated" to be enforceable as judgments. That specific proposition is established primarily through California case law and court procedure (the mechanics of presenting a stipulated judgment for entry), not a single codified rule — this clause states only what these two statutes actually say, and does not claim more. This is one state's statutory and procedural framework, used as real evidence that a private settlement and a court judgment are legally distinct things — not a claim about which state's law or procedure governs a specific marital settlement agreement; procedures for converting a signed agreement into an enforceable judgment vary by state and by court.

NEED-BASED ATTORNEY'S FEES TO ENSURE PARITY OF ACCESS
In a proceeding for dissolution, nullity, or legal separation, a court is directed to ensure that each party has access to legal representation, including early in the proceedings, by ordering one party, if necessary based on income and needs assessments, to pay the other party or the other party's attorney a reasonable amount for attorney's fees and costs of the proceeding.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "In a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, nullity of marriage, or legal separation of the parties, and in any proceeding subsequent to entry of a related judgment, the court shall ensure that each party has access to legal representation, including access early in the proceedings, to preserve each party's rights by ordering, if necessary based on the income and needs assessments, one party, except a governmental entity, to pay to the other party, or to the other party's attorney, whatever amount is reasonably necessary for attorney's fees and for the cost of maintaining or defending the proceeding during the pendency of the proceeding."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2030(a) (California Legislative Information text), the need-based attorney's fee standard (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2030.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a need-based attorney's-fee mechanism in dissolution proceedings — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marital settlement agreement. Whether such fee-shifting exists at all, and on what terms, varies by state; this clause states the statutory standard only and does not address whether it would apply to any specific case. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 2030(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

SIGNATURES
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the parties have executed this agreement on the dates indicated below.

Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

Morgan Casey Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________
